name: SD Card

claims.claim_text: An SD card is not raw flash but a managed device: a controller inside the card performs wear levelling and block remapping that the host cannot see or schedule, so the time an individual write takes is not deterministic.
claims.quote_verbatim: flash is unpredictable how long it will take because they have, like, load balancing stuff inside the SD cards
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The internal housekeeping of an SD card can stall the interface for far longer than a normal transfer; pauses on the order of 200 milliseconds have been observed while the card performs its own management work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've seen really weird stuff happening where the whole SD card is just freezing for 200 milliseconds because it's thinking
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: A FAT filesystem layered on an SD card adds its own latency spikes on top of the card's internal behaviour, because updating a file also forces a rewrite of the allocation table.
claims.quote_verbatim: especially if you have a FAT file system, that can take also time when you have to rewrite the FAT table
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Because the duration of an SD card write is unbounded from the host's point of view, a logging task that writes to a card cannot be run cooperatively alongside time-critical control code; it must be preemptible so that higher-priority tasks such as actuator control still meet their deadlines.
claims.quote_verbatim: logging to an SD card. This can take forever
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: An SD card can be driven over SPI, which lets a filesystem layer sit on top of a generic SPI driver rather than on a dedicated card controller; the hardware abstraction below the filesystem is just the SPI peripheral and its pin assignment.
claims.quote_verbatim: your fat file system is talking to the actual SD card. You do that at the spy layer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: SPI mode needs only four pins and is available on essentially every microcontroller, which makes it the portable way to attach a card; the cost is that it forgoes the wider, faster native SD bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: Four pins for spy. And everyone's going to have support for spy.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Adding mass storage to a microcontroller design is cheap in effort because the card can be talked to over SPI, so the presence of file storage in a specification is not on its own a reason to move up to a larger operating system.
claims.quote_verbatim: So SD cards, you can spy to them if you're willing to.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Card-reader and FAT components pulled into a bare RTOS are nominally free but are unvetted and may need porting to the target; the same function taken from a vendor-backed hardware abstraction layer arrives already exercised across multiple silicon families.
claims.quote_verbatim: You get the SD card reader for quote unquote free, but like, it's not vetted by all of the different vendors and it's, you know, you might have to port it to your system.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Modifying a card's contents from a desktop computer -- deleting, renaming or adding files -- can leave the embedded device that owns the card unable to write to it again, because the device depends on the on-card structures being exactly as it left them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you touch any of the files on the SD card, if you delete a video file, if you, um, uh, rename them, if you, uh, if you copy another file on there, if you do anything at all, touch that card, write to it in any way, shape or form
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: The failure is silent and intermittent: the device continues to display every indication of normal operation while nothing is committed to the card, so the loss is only discovered when the card is next read.
claims.quote_verbatim: The camera can screw up, not always, but it can completely screw up and refuse to record video to that SD card, even though it's telling you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: Data written to a card is not known to exist until it has been read back; the only defence against silent write failure is to verify by reading, on the same principle that an unrestored backup is not a backup.
claims.quote_verbatim: a backup isn't really a backup until you try and back it up until you try and restore it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: Read-back verification after writing a card is routinely skipped because modern flash almost never fails visibly, which is precisely what makes the rare failure so expensive when it happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: You write your file to your SD card, and you don't bother doing a verification check.

claims.claim_text: Removing power from a running system whose root filesystem is on an SD card can corrupt that filesystem; how often this is actually seen in the field varies sharply between practitioners, so it is a risk to be designed against rather than a certainty.
claims.quote_verbatim: using an SD card is always, oh, it's so unreliable and blah, blah, blah. If you turn off the power, it'll corrupt it
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: A card-based firmware update path should be validated destructively by pulling the card out part-way through the update and confirming the device still boots, rather than by assuming the write completes.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've pulled out the SD card during the update and it just happily
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Streaming a long job to a machine over USB risks buffer underruns that corrupt the output; running the same job from a card in the machine removes the host link from the real-time path.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to print directly from the SD card because it can't stream from the USB. It loses the buffer sync and, you know, buffer underruns and screw things up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Putting a micro SD card on a motion-control module decouples program size from the controller's RAM and from the reliability of a streaming link: the job is uploaded once over the network onto the card and then executed locally.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have virtually infinite capacity to serve material from an SD card through that web page
claims.speaker: Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Where a product already has a card slot, distributing firmware as a file on the card is chosen over a wireless update path because the wireless route requires building an update stack that does not otherwise exist.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's an SD card. So you put on the micro SD card and put it in.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The economics of card-based updating rest on vendor-supplied code: the silicon vendor already ships both a card-reading library and a firmware bootloader, so the update mechanism is largely integration rather than development.
claims.quote_verbatim: ST already provide a library that reads an SD card. Right. So they've done that. And also, uh, they've already written the bootloader stuff for loading firmware.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A manual update that requires opening a battery cover and removing the card is an acceptable burden for a product whose firmware is revised rarely; update ergonomics should be weighted by expected update frequency.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't upgrade firmware all the time. So having to, you know, take the battery cover off and take out the SD card is not really, you know, it's hardly a big deal
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Loading application firmware from a card makes every application-level defect field-recoverable; the residual unrecoverable risks are confined to the bootloader itself and to the hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: Any firmware issue I can fix with the soft, with the SD card update.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Booting firmware from a removable card means a bad image is repaired by rewriting the card rather than by returning the unit, which makes it far less risky to ship early hardware with immature software.
claims.quote_verbatim: the firmware started an SD card just like a Raspberry Pi, so updating it is no problem
claims.speaker: David Kronstein

claims.claim_text: Small-batch provisioning of card-booted devices is done by cloning one prepared card image to every unit and then applying only the per-unit configuration, such as a channel assignment, afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: all I've got to do is copy the SD card over to each one and program, and individually set up the channel on each one
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Handing out prepared card images with a fixed single-board computer target removes the first hours of a hands-on course, which otherwise go on reconciling drivers and tool installations across each attendee's own laptop.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can even rock up somewhere and hand out SD cards and plug them in and go
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: Card-imaging tooling converged on cross-platform writers, replacing the earlier situation in which the procedure for writing a boot image differed between Windows, Linux and macOS.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a good utility called etcher.io that is multi-platform.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Boards designed around a keyboard-and-monitor first boot must have their headless configuration written into the card image before first power-up; discovering the requirement afterwards means re-imaging the card repeatedly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you better get that config file, right? Or you're going to be rewriting your SD card a bunch
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: An application processor with a mature boot ROM and build-system support can bring up Linux from an SD card with no on-board storage at all, which is why boot-media and build-system support matter as much as the silicon when selecting such a part.
claims.quote_verbatim: I plugged an SD card into it. I turned it on and it just booted right up
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Consumer SD cards are judged insufficiently reliable for equipment left running unattended; industrial-grade cards are a genuine step up, but for industrial environments the storage is more often moved onto the board itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: SD cards are just not reliable enough. You know, there's like the industrial ones. Okay. Those are better.

claims.claim_text: The Lite variant of a compute module omits on-board managed flash entirely, so the carrier board must provide an external card socket; the non-Lite variants carry soldered flash instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is the CM4, the compute module for Lite. And that actually has no solid state on board. And so then you actually have to have an external SD card.

claims.claim_text: Experience of shipping a card-booted embedded Linux consumer product, where cards died in the field and an operating system and software stack had to be maintained, leads to a preference for a microcontroller with a wireless module for projects that do not genuinely need Linux.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been through the Ninja blocks and I've learned my lessons when it comes to SD cards that die, having projects where you actually have to manage an operating system and a software stack
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A user-accessible card slot punches an opening through the enclosure and therefore through the isolation barrier, which is why an exposed slot is difficult to reconcile with high-voltage safety qualification on measurement instruments.
claims.quote_verbatim: that one was a bit difficult because we had attempted to expose the SD card to the user
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Calculated isolation margin is not the same as tested margin: a design that had margin on paper withstood only two and a half seconds of a required five-second high-voltage exposure after the degradation caused by earlier tests in the sequence, and the user-accessible card slot was sealed as a result.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, you have to survive that for five seconds. We survived it for two and a half after, uh, degradation from previous testing.
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: The safety qualification sequence preconditions the disassembled unit at 93 percent relative humidity for 48 hours, reassembles it, wraps it in foil and applies a 5,400 volt stress, so any aperture in the enclosure is judged after the insulation has absorbed moisture rather than when dry.
claims.quote_verbatim: they put in a sauna for 48 hours. So, it's 93% relative humidity
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A rugged battery-powered logger can keep the card entirely inside the sealed enclosure and expose only a USB port for offload, which avoids both the ingress path of a user-accessible slot and the handling wear of repeated card insertion.
claims.quote_verbatim: just takes a GPS feed, records it to an SD card inside. Um, and then you can download the logs later over USB.
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: The volume at which SD cards are manufactured can make a complete, controller-managed card cheaper than the bare flash die it contains, to the point that finished cards are reflowed directly onto product boards as the storage component.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've seen the SD cards soldered directly to the boards. Actually reflowed directly to the boards because it's cheaper than buying the raw chip.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Clap on, clap off, lights flicker

claims.claim_text: Consumer products are found using an ordinary SD card fixed permanently to the board with silicone rather than a socket, taking the card's cost advantage while removing the socket, its cost and its mechanical failure path.
claims.quote_verbatim: the storage mechanism was a SD card that was, like, RTV'd to the board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Clap on, clap off, lights flicker

claims.claim_text: Full-size SD sockets have become the harder part to source as the market moved to micro form factors, so a design that wants the full-size outline must plan for connector availability.
claims.quote_verbatim: Everything switched to mini or micro or whatever it is.
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: The SD card outline is large enough to be used as a carrier for a complete system-in-package: earlier commercial wireless cards fitted into it were restricted in compute and closed to user code, whereas a system-in-package built into the same outline can run Linux and arbitrary firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: These things have been around for quite some time. But they are quite limited in their compute power. And also you can't run custom code on that.
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Simulating a card faithfully means synthesising a real FAT image from the supplied files, because the firmware under simulation issues the same filesystem reads it would issue against physical media.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a FAT file system driver. So if you simulate an SD card and upload files to that simulated SD card
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked

claims.claim_text: Logging instruments write to the card in plain FAT rather than a private format so that the card can be pulled and read directly on any computer without a vendor tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's just a fat format so it actually logs data to the SD card and, yeah, it's just a standard fat format
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Clap on, clap off, lights flicker

claims.claim_text: Holding a device's operating system on a removable card instead of in on-chip flash makes the entire firmware image trivially extractable by anyone who opens the case and reads the card.
claims.quote_verbatim: it actually has an SD card in there containing the operating system. It's not built into the chip.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Cards displace obsolete removable media in reimplementations of old systems because the original drives and discs are both unreliable and hard to buy, and one card holds what previously required a shelf of media and minutes of load time.
claims.quote_verbatim: The original hardware is unreliable. And the floppy drives are crap.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Apple HQ and Vintage Arcade Games - The Mothership Manifesto

claims.claim_text: Local card storage is what allows speech recognition to run entirely offline on a small board: a four gigabyte card carries a two gigabyte pronunciation dictionary against which spoken sentences are decomposed into phonemes.
claims.quote_verbatim: the board has a four gig SD card on which two gig is the dictionary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland of Audeme
